reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive defect of the SLC25A20 inner-membrane carrier that exchanges long-chain acylcarnitine into the matrix for free carnitine out
Most cases present in the neonatal period with a severe, often life-threatening crisis: hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia, hepatic dysfunction and hyperammonaemia
Cardiac arrhythmia and conduction disturbance can dominate and cause sudden collapse
Biochemically resembles CPT2 deficiency, with elevated long-chain acylcarnitines (C16, C18:1) and low free carnitine
A minority with residual carrier activity have a milder phenotype with better survival
Acute management provides high-dose intravenous glucose to suppress lipolysis, avoids fasting, and supports cardiac and hepatic function
Chronic care uses long-chain fat restriction with medium-chain triglyceride substitution, frequent feeds and a strict emergency regimen
reference.pathophysiology: The carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase is the inner mitochondrial membrane antiporter that imports long-chain acylcarnitine into the matrix in exchange for free carnitine, an essential step of the carnitine cycle linking CPT1 and CPT2. When the carrier is deficient, long-chain fatty acids cannot reach the matrix for beta-oxidation, so heart, muscle and liver are deprived of fatty-acid-derived energy during fasting or stress and ketogenesis fails. Accumulation of long-chain acylcarnitines is arrhythmogenic and cardiotoxic, accounting for the prominent cardiac features, and impaired acetyl-CoA generation contributes to hyperammonaemia.
additionalDifferentials: Carnitine palmitoyltransferase II deficiency (very similar biochemistry)
Neonatal cardiomyopathy or arrhythmia of other cause
Sepsis or inborn errors presenting with neonatal hyperammonaemia
Long-chain hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase / trifunctional protein deficiency
additionalInvestigations: Plasma acylcarnitine profile with elevated long-chain acylcarnitines (C16, C18:1) and low free carnitine
Blood glucose, ketones, ammonia, lactate and liver function during crisis
ECG and echocardiography for arrhythmia and cardiomyopathy
SLC25A20 molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis
Fibroblast fatty-acid oxidation flux or transport studies
Creatine kinase where rhabdomyolysis is suspected
redFlags: Neonatal cardiac arrhythmia or conduction block with haemodynamic instability
Hypoketotic hypoglycaemia with encephalopathy and hyperammonaemia
Recurrent life-threatening decompensation during intercurrent illness
reference.prognosis: The neonatal-onset severe form carries high mortality despite intensive treatment, whereas individuals with residual carrier activity and milder disease can survive with careful metabolic management; early diagnosis and aggressive prevention of catabolism are critical.
pitfalls: Mistaking the biochemistry for CPT2 deficiency without confirmatory genetics
Under-treating catabolism, allowing lipolysis to drive cardiac toxicity
Overlooking arrhythmia as the presenting feature of metabolic collapse
Permitting any fasting in a diagnosed infant
references: Scriver's OMMBID (Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease)
management: Prevent catabolism as the cornerstone: avoid fasting and provide frequent carbohydrate-rich feeds with a written emergency regimen during intercurrent illness
Restrict long-chain fat and supplement with medium-chain triglycerides, which bypass the defective carnitine cycle
During acute crises give intravenous glucose to suppress lipolysis and support cardiac, hepatic and metabolic function
Monitor and treat arrhythmia and conduction disturbance, which can dominate and cause sudden collapse
Monitor with acylcarnitine profile, glucose, ammonia and cardiac assessment
Manage within a specialist metabolic team
Offer SLC25A20 genetic confirmation, counselling and family or newborn screening, given autosomal recessive inheritance
